newsitem.title: UK: Losers hard to find after WTO telephone pact.
newsitem.headline: Losers hard to find after WTO telephone pact.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Liberalisation of the world's telephone markets, agreed by World Trade Organisation members, will boost companies which have already formed global alliances, analysts said on Monday.
Concert Communications Services, the combination between British Telecommunications and MCI Communications Corp of the U.S., was said to have the inside track in the battle for new markets.
Telecommunications experts were hard pressed to find anyone but winners after the new agreeement was hammered out by about 70 countries in Geneva, Switzerland, this weekend.
Experts said smaller firms would benefit too. But most of all consumers across the world would be more likely to have enhanced telephone networks early in the next century.

Even nations which used telephone monopolies as a form of taxation, gouging extra revenue from high tariffs, would probably decide that more money could be raised by cutting prices and boosting business, they said.

According to research consultancy Dataquest, the world telecommunications market was worth more than $800 billion last year. The U.S. has the highest telephone penetration, with 61 per 100 people. Western Europe has 45 per 100, Dataquest says.
This underlines the huge potential in developing nations.

"Two thirds of the world's population have never made a phone call. Lack of access means that no less than half of the earth's inhabitants cannot make a phone call even if they wanted to," said Michael Masin, president international of GTE Corp said in a recent magazine article.
"The world has 600 million phone lines for some 5.6 billion people - just under 10 people per phone line," Masin said.

Liberalised telephone markets have led to slashed prices and enhanced services in pioneer nations like the U.S. and Britain. Most European Union nations begin shaking off state monopoly powers at the end of this year.

In anticipation of this, and with an eye on developing markets, many big national companies have joined forces. BT and MCI formed Concert. Global One International linked Sprint Corp, Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom. AT&T and various state companies formed WorldPartners.

"Concert is well placed, AT&T and its partners less well placed. AT&T is not executing well in Europe, it's losing senior people, and having to focus back on the U.S. where it's beginning to see local competition," said Nigel Deighton, research director at U.S. technology consultancy Gartner Group.

"And Global One, as their home markets open up next year, that will take some focus on their part that could have been devoted internationally. Concert is the one that may gain the most (from liberalisation)," Deighton said.
Deighton said many companies outside alliances will benefit, like WorldCom and Equant, and equipment makers like Alcatel, Siemens, Ericsson and Nokia.
Gillian Marcelle, consultant for telecoms researcher Analysys, also sees widespread gains from the pact.

"Companies that already have expertise in international markets like Telefonica de Espana SA are well placed in Latin America. Companies which can capitalise on local contacts and have worked on relationships are equally well suited," said Marcelle.
"What the WTO deal does is provide increased momentum for market opening, and also provides stable conditions and sets forth a set of regulatory frameworks for liberalising markets," Marcelle said.
